correctness.rationale: Exact diamond-section integration gives \(\Phi(0)=\Phi^{\prime}(0)=0\) and \(\Phi^{\prime\prime}(r)\ge4[1-(v^2+w^2)r^2/2]\), strictly positive in the interior of \(r\in[0,1]\) for \(v^2+w^2\le2\). Two valid integrations by parts yield strictly positive axial cosine transforms at every nonzero axial frequency, and positivity at zero frequency follows directly. An explicit diagonal Fourier-zero identity proves nonemptiness; closedness ensures a minimizing zero and strict \(\kappa(P_a)>\sqrt2\). Exact volume and equal-volume ball formulas give sufficient threshold \(\pi j^3/(2\sqrt2)\). The included rational script checks \(G(x_0)<-3/10000\) and its rational parameter comparison below \(101\); Taylor alternating remainder and monotonicity identify the first positive zero \(j<x_0\). Six vertices are minimal by antipodal spanning pairs.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The general failure of ball maximality is already known, and no novelty is claimed for that. The published disk-bipyramid estimates rely on Bessel radial-section transforms, not the two-variable transform for a diamond section, and do not imply this theorem without a substantive new calculation.

originality.rationale: Relevant primary full text and three nearest published comparison texts were inspected. Existing counterexamples and quantitative zero-free strips concern disks of revolution and do not imply an integer-coordinate six-vertex polyhedral witness. The asserted new content is the minimal-vertex polyhedral Fourier-zero violation and its proved diamond-section cylinder, not the known generic failure of ball maximality. Unindexed anisotropic-octahedron priority remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: Classical, unindexed or unpublished treatments of the Fourier transform of stretched octahedra could independently contain this six-vertex obstruction.
The quantitative certificate does not establish the exact first Fourier zero or an optimal stretching threshold.

value.rationale: The problem has a natural combinatorial refinement: determine the least vertex complexity at which a centrally symmetric polytope can violate ball extremality. The six-vertex lower bound is intrinsic (three spanning antipodal pairs), and the witness achieves it with integral coordinates and a completely explicit curvature-based zero-free proof. This remains meaningful even though smoother convex-body counterexamples and nonminimal finite approximations were known.
